design_detail: Sponsor's secondary analysis of pooled individual data from four randomized, double-blind phase 2 trials of MDMA-assisted psychotherapy for chronic PTSD (MP-8 and MP-12 in the United States, MP-4 in Canada, MP-9 in Israel; NCT01958593, NCT01211405, NCT01689740, NCT01793610; data collected January 2012 to March 2017), the four of six phase 2 trials that included the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index. Blinded comparison at the primary endpoint (1 to 2 months after two blinded sessions): participants pooled into an 'active' group (75 to 125 mg MDMA, n = 47) and a 'control' group (0 to 40 mg, n = 16) by unstratified t tests; then, after unblinding and open-label crossover, an uncontrolled mixed-model analysis of all participants at treatment exit and 12-month follow-up. Analyses not preregistered. An expression of concern (jts_2025a) and a correction (jts_2025b) were published on 3 December 2024; the correction removed the four MP-4 participants treated by a pair of therapists involved in an ethical violation, leaving 59 (45 active, 14 control at 25 to 40 mg, no inactive placebo). Read as the PMC copy (CC BY-NC), with both notices read in full.
can_establish: Whether self-reported sleep quality improved more over 1 to 2 months after two sessions with full-dose MDMA than with low-dose MDMA in these trials, as reanalysed after the correction, and how sleep and PTSD scores changed, without a comparison group, to 12 months after open-label treatment.
cannot_establish: An effect of MDMA on sleep separate from expectancy (blinding was not assessed and the outcome is self-reported), any effect at 12 months (everyone had received full-dose MDMA by then), or objective sleep changes; and, after the expression of concern, it cannot be taken as independent of the sponsor's handling of the MP-4 site.

sample.recruitment: Referrals by health professionals, internet advertisements and word of mouth; civilians, veterans and first responders aged 18 or older with an inadequate response to at least one pharmacotherapy or psychotherapy; three private-practice sites and one government-funded psychiatric hospital (Method › Participants and Procedure, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: PTSD for at least 6 months and CAPS-IV total severity of 50 or more (MP-8, MP-12, MP-9) or 60 or more (MP-4); anxiety and depression allowed; excluded: past or current psychotic disorders, bipolar I, borderline personality disorder, eating disorders with active purging, substance use disorder within 60 days (6 months for MP-4), major medical conditions except controlled hypertension or treated hypothyroidism, pregnancy, lactation or no effective contraception, weight under 48 kg. Psychiatric medicines were tapered and stopped, except as-needed anxiolytics and sedative-hypnotics between sessions, gabapentin for pain and ADHD medicines (Participants and Procedure, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs).
sample.demographics: Original sample (63): mean age 40.8 (SD 11.5); 34 men (54.0%); 85.7% White; mean PTSD duration 225 months; combat trauma 71.4%; lifetime suicidal ideation 87.3%; earlier ecstasy use 28.6% (Results › Sample Characteristics; Table 1). The groups differed: combat trauma 100% of controls and 61.7% of the active group, PTSD duration 155 against 249 months. The corrected Table 1 gives other trauma figures (combat 37.3% of 59), which cannot follow from removing four people (see reporting issues).
sample.attrition: Modified intention-to-treat set: participants with at least one blinded session and at least one follow-up assessment; one participant without a baseline PSQI was omitted. The PSQI was added by amendment in MP-8, so 6 of 26 MP-8 participants have no PSQI; PSQI at the primary endpoint for 45 of 47 active participants (Participants and Procedure, 6th paragraph; Data Analysis, 1st paragraph; Table 2 note).
sample.selection_effects: Treatment-resistant volunteers; a large share combat veterans and first responders; 28.6% had used ecstasy before. Pooling trials with different allocation ratios and control doses produced groups that differ at baseline. The correction removed four participants of one site because of an ethical violation by their therapists.

exposure.measurement: Assigned study drug in two blinded 8-hour sessions 3 to 5 weeks apart, each followed by three 90-minute integrative sessions, after three 90-minute preparatory sessions with a co-therapist team, using the sponsor's manual; overnight stay with a night attendant. After unblinding at the primary endpoint, full-dose participants (except in MP-9) had one more open-label session, and control and 75 mg participants crossed over to two (MP-9) or three open-label full-dose sessions (Participants and Procedure, 4th to 6th paragraphs).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as printed: by mouth; active doses 75, 100 or 125 mg, control doses 0, 25, 30 or 40 mg (25, 30 or 40 mg after the correction), each followed by an optional supplemental half dose; MDMA from David Nichols, Purdue University (MP-8, MP-12) or Lipomed (MP-4, MP-9), in equivalent-weight capsules with lactose.
exposure.polysubstance: Substance use disorder in the previous 60 days (6 months for MP-4) excluded. Prior ecstasy use 18.8% of controls and 31.9% of the active group (Table 1). Sleep aids on the nights of blinded sessions were given only in the active group: 6 of 46 after session 1 and 5 of 46 after session 2 (Results › Blinded Endpoint, 3rd paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; the primary endpoint was 1 to 2 months after the second blinded session.

comparison.controls: Pooled 'control' group: participants randomized within their trial to 0, 25, 30 or 40 mg MDMA with the same psychotherapy (after the correction only 25 to 40 mg: the removed MP-4 participants were the only ones on 0 mg). The 75 mg group, counted as active in the blinded comparison, also crossed over to open-label full doses.
comparison.matching: Randomized within each trial, but the pooled comparison uses unstratified independent-samples t tests across trials with different allocation ratios and control doses; the groups were defined by the protocols' dose designations and 'by inspection of posttreatment CAPS-IV scores' (Data Analysis, 1st paragraph), citing the pooled phase 2 analysis by Mithoefer et al. (2019), retracted in 2024.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the randomized comparison within trials; across the pooled groups trauma type and PTSD duration differ (Table 1). Expectancy was not measured.

outcomes.instruments: PSQI (19 items, seven components, global score 0 to 21; past month), at baseline, primary endpoint, treatment exit and 12 months; CAPS-IV (0 to 136) rated by an independent rater who was not present during the psychotherapy sessions (Measures).
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors cite a cut-off of 5 for poor sleep and adopt a 3-point drop as clinically meaningful; Cronbach's alpha in this sample .63 at baseline, .71, .69 and .80 later (corrected .65, .72, .70, .80).
outcomes.operationalization: Improvement in sleep quality: larger fall in the PSQI global score from baseline to primary endpoint in the active group; a 3-point drop counted as clinically meaningful.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: CAPS and PSQI totals, seven PSQI components, the 3-point responder comparison, the three open-label mixed-model contrasts and the CAPS-PSQI correlation, plus covariate screening, all at alpha 0.05.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: The CAPS-IV rater was independent of the therapy; the PSQI is self-reported. Blinding of participants was not assessed.

analysis.effect_sizes: Original: CAPS-IV change −34.0 (SD 26.5) active against −12.4 (16.4) control, p = .003, Hedges' g 0.88 printed with 95% CI −5.18 to 6.93; PSQI change −3.53 (5.03) against +0.56 (3.05), p = .003, g 0.88 printed with CI −0.27 to 2.03 (Table 2). Editors' recalculation from Table 2: g 0.88 with 95% CI 0.29 to 1.47 for CAPS-IV and 0.28 to 1.47 for PSQI. Corrected (jts_2025b): CAPS-IV −34.93 (26.66) against −11.07 (16.85), g 0.96 (0.33 to 1.59); PSQI −3.51 (5.08) against +0.50 (3.25), p = .008, g 0.85 (0.23 to 1.47); 3-point PSQI response 24 of 45 (53.3%) against 2 of 14 (14.3%). Open-label (corrected, N = 58): PSQI least-squares means 12.59, 8.18 at treatment exit and 7.09 at 12 months; treatment exit to 12 months −1.09 (SE 0.49), p = .029; CAPS-IV 88.22, 42.46 and 35.28.
analysis.covariates: Original mixed model: time, baseline CAPS-IV and study as fixed effects, participant random; candidate covariates (age, PTSD duration, sex, race, prior ecstasy use) screened one at a time at p ≤ .01; age retained (p = .017). The correction drops baseline CAPS-IV and study from the base model and reports that no candidate covariate met the cut-off.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Open Practices Statement: the four trials were registered, but the analyses were not formally preregistered; the article nonetheless carries a 'Preregistered Research Designs' badge linked to the trial registrations.
analysis.selective_reporting: Grouping of doses partly by inspection of post-treatment CAPS-IV scores. The correction removed the subgroup result (a 3-point PSQI drop predicting lower CAPS-IV at treatment exit and 12 months) because it was no longer significant at treatment exit, without reporting the 12-month result, and changed the model specification.
analysis.power: None; the authors state the pilot trials were not powered for this exploratory analysis.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In four pooled phase 2 trials of one sponsor, self-reported sleep quality improved more 1 to 2 months after two blinded sessions in the full-dose group than in the low-dose (and, originally, placebo) group: by about 4 PSQI points, with half of the full-dose group improving by 3 points or more against one in seven controls. After open-label full-dose treatment for all, scores were lower again at 12 months than at treatment exit by about 1 point, without a comparison group. The outcome is self-reported, blinding was not assessed, and the data were corrected in 2024 after an ethical violation at one site.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the trials provide evidence for beneficial effects of MDMA-assisted psychotherapy in treating sleep disturbance. The Discussion calls the change from treatment exit to 12 months an enduring, clinically meaningful benefit, although that change (about 1 point) is below the authors' own 3-point threshold and comes from uncontrolled open-label data, and suggests the therapy may be "particularly suited for promoting sleep regulation" (Discussion, 8th paragraph). The correction states that removing the data "does not compromise the conclusions", although one subgroup result disappeared.

timeline.event: The first phase 2 trial's follow-up reports improved sleep on a questionnaire item in 12 of 19 participants (Mithoefer et al., 2013).
Pooled analysis of six phase 2 trials (Mithoefer et al., 2019), cited here for the dose grouping and for insomnia rates; retracted on 10 August 2024.
This pooled sleep analysis (published online 10 June 2021).

Expression of concern and correction (3 December 2024): the four MP-4 participants treated by two therapists involved in an ethical violation are removed; the journal judges the authors' non-disclosure improper.

replication.where_it_stands: The only analysis of sleep in the MDMA trials found here. It rests on the sponsor's own pooled data, carries an expression of concern, and cites a retracted pooled analysis for its dose grouping; its blinded comparison is with low-dose MDMA after the correction. Cite the corrected figures, with the notice.

funding.funder: Not stated as a funding statement. The trials were run by MAPS and MAPS Public Benefit Corporation (copyright of the article is held by MAPS Public Benefit Corporation).
funding.declared_conflicts: Author note: Ponte previously received salary support from MAPS as a full-time employee; Jerome is a full-time employee of MAPS Public Benefit Corporation; Hamilton received salary support from MAPS PBC as a biostatistician; Mithoefer received research funds from MAPS PBC as investigator, medical monitor and trainer; Yazar-Klosinski is a full-time employee of MAPS; Feduccia is a full-time employee of MAPS PBC; Vermetten received salary support from MAPS PBC as an investigator.
funding.affiliations_note: Every author is or was paid by the sponsor. The corresponding author is on the MAPS PBC Safety Team. Jerome, Mithoefer and Feduccia are authors of all three phase 2 analyses retracted in August 2024, and Hamilton and Yazar-Klosinski of two of them (author lists in the Crossref records of the three retraction notes).

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial with sleep as a prespecified outcome, an active placebo, assessment of blinding and expectancy, objective sleep measures (actigraphy or polysomnography) and a controlled follow-up beyond the end of treatment, run independently of the sponsor.

domains.note: Each trial was randomized, but the pooled comparison is unstratified across trials with different allocation ratios and control doses, producing baseline imbalances (combat trauma 100% against 61.7%; PTSD duration 155 against 249 months).
Participants and therapists probably knew the dose from its effects (not assessed); sleep aids on session nights only in the active group.
PSQI missing for 6 of 26 MP-8 participants (added by amendment) and for two active participants at the primary endpoint; the open-label analyses rely on a mixed model.
The PSQI is self-reported and participants probably knew their dose; expectancy was not measured.
Analyses not preregistered; dose groups defined partly by inspecting post-treatment CAPS-IV scores; the correction changed the model and dropped a subgroup result.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The blinded comparison rests on randomization within trials, but its outcome is self-reported with probable unblinding and its analysis choices were made without a plan, partly after inspecting outcomes. The 12-month results are uncontrolled. The expression of concern and the correction add that one site's data were affected by an ethical violation that the authors did not disclose at submission. Cite the corrected blinded comparison for a short-term difference in self-reported sleep against low-dose MDMA, with these caveats, and the open-label results only descriptively.

key_findings.finding: Four randomized, double-blind phase 2 trials at four sites (MP-8, MP-12 in the United States; MP-4 in Canada; MP-9 in Israel), data collected January 2012 to March 2017; the two earliest phase 2 trials did not include the PSQI and are not in this analysis. Original pooled sample 63: 47 active (75 to 125 mg) and 16 control (0 to 40 mg).
key_findings.locator: Method › Participants and Procedure, 1st paragraph; Abstract; Data Analysis, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: After the 2024 correction: 59 (45 active, 14 control at 25 to 40 mg); see sc_jts_2025b.

key_findings.finding: Dose groups were pooled according to the trials' designation of doses as control or active and by inspection of post-treatment CAPS-IV scores, citing the pooled analysis by Mithoefer et al. (2019), which the reference list in PMC marks as retracted; blinded comparisons used independent-samples t tests, with no power analysis.
key_findings.locator: Method › Data Analysis, 1st paragraph; References (Mithoefer et al., 2019)

key_findings.finding: Original blinded endpoint (1 to 2 months after the second blinded session): CAPS-IV change −33.98 (SD 26.46) active against −12.38 (16.38) control, p = .003; PSQI change −3.53 (5.03) against +0.56 (3.05), p = .003, Hedges' g 0.88 for both; 3-point PSQI drop in 25 active (printed 53.2%) against 2 controls (12.5%), χ2 8.87, N = 61, p = .003.
key_findings.locator: Results › Blinded Endpoint, 1st paragraph; Table 2 and its notes
key_findings.note: Superseded by the corrected values (sc_jts_2025b). The printed confidence intervals for g are wrong (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: PSQI components at the blinded endpoint (original): sleep quality −0.62 against +0.19 (p = .006), sleep latency −0.42 against +0.38 (p = .005), daytime dysfunction −0.82 against +0.25 (p < .001); duration, efficiency, disturbance and use of sleep medication not significantly different.

On the nights of blinded sessions, no control participant received a sleep aid; in the active group (n = 46) 3 received zolpidem, 2 melatonin and 1 zopiclone after session 1, and 4 zolpidem and 1 melatonin after session 2.

Open-label analysis of everyone (original, N = 62): CAPS-IV least-squares mean 88.50 at baseline, 42.97 at treatment exit and 36.43 at 12 months (exit to 12 months −6.53, SE 2.50, p = .011); PSQI 12.65, 8.37 and 7.34 (exit to 12 months −1.03, SE 0.46, p = .029); 21 participants had a PSQI of 5 or lower at 12 months against 2 at baseline; change in CAPS-IV and PSQI from baseline to treatment exit correlated r = .371 (n = 58).
key_findings.locator: Results › Open-Label Endpoints: Treatment Exit and Long-Term Follow-Up, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 3; Figure 3 legend
key_findings.note: Uncontrolled: all had received full-dose MDMA by then. Corrected values in sc_jts_2025b.

key_findings.finding: The CAPS-IV sleep items were not removed, so part of the CAPS-PSQI correlation is built into the measures, as the authors note; limitations named: small, mostly White sample (85.7%), self-reported outcomes.
key_findings.locator: Results › Blinded Endpoint, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Open Practices Statement: the four trials were registered (NCT01958593, NCT01211405, NCT01689740, NCT01793610); the analyses were not formally preregistered; data available only through a data-use proposal to MAPS.
Every author was paid by MAPS or MAPS PBC (author note); no separate funding statement is printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The 95% confidence intervals printed for Hedges' g in the original Table 2 do not fit the effect sizes or the p values: CAPS-IV g 0.88 with CI −5.18 to 6.93 and PSQI g 0.88 with CI −0.27 to 2.03 (including zero despite p = .003); sleep efficiency and sleep disturbance have intervals excluding zero (0.05 to 0.70; 0.25 to 0.60) although p = .191 and .124. Editors' recalculation from the table's means, SDs and group sizes: 0.29 to 1.47 (CAPS-IV), 0.28 to 1.47 (PSQI), −0.20 to 0.95 (efficiency), −0.18 to 0.97 (disturbance).
reporting_issues.consequence: The original intervals cannot be used; the corrected Table 2 (jts_2025b) gives plausible intervals.

reporting_issues.issue: The share of active participants with a 3-point PSQI drop is printed as 53.2% (25 of 47) and 42.6% (20 of 47) for the rest, which add to 95.7%; only 45 active participants had PSQI data, so the share is 25 of 45 (55.6%). The corrected footnote repeats the pattern: 24 (53.3%) and 19 (42.2%) use 45 as denominator although the table gives n = 44 and the counts add to 43; the printed χ2 of 6.85 could not be reproduced from those counts (editors' calculation 7.34, or 5.76 with continuity correction).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Results › Blinded Endpoint, 1st paragraph; Table 2 note b); correction, Table 2 note b
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite counts rather than these percentages; the direction of the difference is not in doubt.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 (original) prints unlabelled counts and percentages (27, 44.3%; 34, 55.7%) beside the baseline and treatment-exit CAPS rows, while the rows for a 3-point PSQI drop to 12 months are empty; the numbers appear to belong to those empty rows. The corrected Table 3 gives 35 (60.3%) yes and 15 (25.9%) no, percentages of N = 58 although only 50 have data (35 of 50 is 70%).
reporting_issues.consequence: The 12-month responder figures are unclear in both versions; state counts with their denominator.

reporting_issues.issue: The subgroup differences in CAPS-IV for participants with a 3-point PSQI drop are given as least-squares means with 'SD' 7.06 and 6.00; with p = .046 and p < .001 these are standard errors (editors' check: −14.41/7.06 gives z of about 2.0).
reporting_issues.consequence: Mislabelled; the result was withdrawn in the correction anyway.

reporting_issues.issue: The treatment-exit to 12-month PSQI change is p = .029 in Table 3 and p = .030 in the text and abstract; the primary endpoint is '1 month' after the second blinded session in the Figure 2 note and '1 to 2 months' in the Methods.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Table 3; Results › Open-Label Endpoints, 1st paragraph; Figure 2 note; Method › Participants and Procedure, 6th paragraph)

reporting_issues.issue: The article carries a 'Preregistered Research Designs' badge, while its Open Practices Statement says the analyses were not formally preregistered; the badge links to the trial registrations.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Open Practices Statement; Open Research Badges)
reporting_issues.consequence: The badge should not be read as preregistration of this analysis.

reporting_issues.issue: The analysis relies on a retracted paper: the dose grouping cites Mithoefer et al. (2019), and the Discussion takes insomnia rates on session nights from it (38% control against 29% MDMA, and 47% against 36% the next day; revised in the correction to 34% and 29%, 44% and 31%). The correction (December 2024) describes these revisions as reflecting an ongoing correction of that paper, which had been retracted on 10 August 2024.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Method › Data Analysis, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 4th paragraph); correction, Discussion changes
reporting_issues.consequence: The insomnia figures from the retracted analysis must not be cited; the grouping method depends on a retracted source.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC8453707 (all sections, Tables 1 to 3 as text, figure legends, Open Practices Statement, author note, article notes, reference list; Figures 1 to 3 are images whose legends only were read; the supplementary table, a .docx file, was not read, its content being reproduced in the correction). Read together with the expression of concern (PMC full text PMC12416979) and the correction (publisher full text, https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jts.23098, free access). Crossref records of all three read in this reader's tab.
